summary: Explains the Internet calendaring and scheduling standards (iCalendar, iTIP, iMIP) and how they relate. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a map to the set of rules that let different calendar programs share events and invitations.

subtitle: Map of the Internet calendaring standards and how they work together.

tldr.problem: Different calendaring and scheduling systems cannot interoperate; organizations and individuals need standard protocols and data formats to share calendar information and coordinate meetings across systems.
tldr.mechanism: Three complementary standards (iCalendar for data format, iTIP for scheduling protocol, iMIP for email transport) and a fourth in development (CAP for real-time access) provide a framework for calendaring and scheduling across the Internet.
tldr.outcome: Standards-based calendaring enables vendors to build compatible products and users to choose different clients without being locked into one vendor's ecosystem.

today: RFC 3283 is an Informational document that remains relevant as the foundational guide to Internet calendaring standards. Today, iCalendar, iTIP and iMIP are widely deployed in email systems, web calendars and mobile applications worldwide. CAP evolved into CalDAV (RFC 4791), which is now the standard for calendar server access and is implemented by major calendar services.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
RFC 3283 is a guide to Internet calendaring and scheduling standards, intended to help developers and architects understand how different protocols work together. It addresses three existing standards—iCalendar (RFC 2445), iTIP (RFC 2446), and iMIP (RFC 2447)—and the emerging Calendar Access Protocol (CAP).

The guide defines essential terminology for understanding calendaring systems. A calendar is a collection of events, to-dos and journal entries that serve as an agenda. A calendar service is a server application providing access to calendar stores. A calendar user (CU) is a person or entity that accesses calendar information, while a calendar user agent (CUA) is the software the user employs to access calendars. A component is a piece of calendar data such as a specific event or to-do item.

The document also covers roles in scheduling: a delegator is a user who assigns their participation in an event to another person (the delegate), while a designate is a user authorized to act on behalf of another.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you understand calendars on the Internet, you need to know the words. A calendar is your schedule. A user is a person. An agent is the app they use. Once you know these words, everything else makes sense.

sections.title: How the Four Standards Relate
sections.content:
iCalendar is the data format—the language used to describe calendar objects. Think of it as analogous to email's RFC 2822: it defines the structure of a calendar message or file.

iTIP (iCalendar Transport-Independent Interoperability Protocol) is the scheduling protocol that uses the iCalendar language to describe scheduling transactions—creating events, accepting invitations, proposing alternative times and responding to requests for free/busy information.

iMIP (iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol) is a transport binding that carries iTIP messages via email. Analogous to SMTP in the email world, iMIP enables scheduling across the Internet using existing email infrastructure.

CAP (Calendar Access Protocol) provides real-time access to a calendar store—similar to how IMAP and POP provide email access. CAP allows a calendar user agent to create calendars, search for events, manage access rights and perform calendar operations beyond basic scheduling.

The relationship is architecturally clean: iCalendar is the data format that all others build on, iTIP is the scheduling protocol (transport-independent), iMIP binds iTIP to email, and CAP provides real-time store access.
sections.plainLanguage: iCalendar is the language calendars use, like English. iTIP is the rules for scheduling meetings, like how to write a polite invitation. iMIP is sending that invitation by email. CAP is a live calendar server you can connect to whenever you want.

sections.title: What Calendaring Systems Need to Do
sections.content:
The document identifies six usage scenarios that motivate the need for standards.

A doctor managing her own calendar needs to read and manipulate her calendar with a single application. A musician with multiple devices needs to access and update her calendar from an Internet-based client and a PDA while maintaining synchronization. A software team needs to share calendar information to schedule meetings across multiple users on the same calendar service. A teacher and students need to schedule office hours and appointments within a calendar system.

The more demanding scenarios require interoperability across system boundaries. A movie theater publishing its schedule to customers must share calendar information with users of different vendors' systems. A social club scheduling meetings with members needs to coordinate across multiple different calendar services, possibly from different vendors.

Some of these needs can be met with proprietary solutions; others cannot. Interoperability across vendors and systems requires open standards for both the data format (iCalendar) and the protocols for scheduling (iTIP) and access (CAP).
sections.plainLanguage: People need to keep track of their own calendars, share schedules with others, and let computers from different companies talk to each other. That's why standards are needed—so all the different calendar apps can work together.

sections.title: Deployment Patterns
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates how these standards apply to different system architectures.

A single-user standalone system needs no protocol at all, though it may use iCalendar as a storage format internally for portability to other applications.

For users with single-user systems communicating, iTIP via iMIP (email-based scheduling) is natural because email is already ubiquitous. This allows users to schedule meetings by sending and receiving calendar messages through their existing email systems.

A single user with multiple devices can synchronize a calendar across a PDA, web client and PC by connecting to a CAP-enabled calendar service. Each device uses CAP to read and update the shared calendar on the server.

For multiple users on the same multi-user system, CAP enables direct access to shared calendars, making it easy to view others' schedules and organize meetings without email latency.

When users on different multi-user systems need to schedule, the systems can coordinate using either CAP or iMIP, depending on whether they choose real-time or email-based communication.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different ways to set up calendars: just for one person, using email to trade invitations, connecting to a server, or connecting two servers together. The standards support all of these.

sections.title: Key Implementation Challenges
sections.content:
The document highlights several important aspects that implementers must consider.

Timezones: Events can be specified in particular time zones. Time zones may be defined centrally or customized per user. Vendors may describe the same time zone differently, requiring care in interoperability.

Transport choice: Implementers must decide between network protocols like CAP (which may require firewall configuration) and email-based protocols like iMIP (which expose time-sensitive data to mail system latency). Each has trade-offs.

Data size: Calendar components may be very large, particularly with attachments. Systems may limit maximum component size and the amount of data that can be downloaded.

Recurring components: The RFC warns that recurring events with complex recurrence rules require careful interpretation to ensure interoperability.

Open issues: Several problems remain unsolved. Meeting scheduling operates on calendar addresses (often email addresses), but people may have multiple calendars in multiple locations, making it difficult to route bookings reliably. Neither iTIP nor CAP addresses user and calendar administration; this remains vendor-specific. Real-time event notification is not provided; clients must poll for changes instead. These gaps could be targets for future standards work.
sections.plainLanguage: When you build a calendar system, you have to think about time zones, email delays, file sizes and repeating events. There are also some problems nobody has solved yet, like knowing which calendar address is really for one person.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that calendar systems handle sensitive scheduling and personal information, requiring careful security design.

Access control: CAP must offer granular configuration options so that only appropriate information is released to requesters. Only authorized users should see sensitive calendar data.

Authentication: Access control must be coupled with strong authentication so the right people see the right information. CAP uses the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) for authentication. iMIP, being email-based, faces challenges since store-and-forward protocols do not typically include authentication; implementers should consider requiring it as a default, using mechanisms such as signing and encryption.

Calendar spam: Because scheduling messages can be sent via email without authentication, email spoofing is trivial and calendar spam is possible. Systems allowing automated request processing should defend against malicious message flooding.

Denial of service: Once these systems become widely deployed, adversaries are likely to exploit the ability to flood calendars with bogus requests, requiring detection and recovery methods.

User experience: The security context should be obvious to users. Because underlying mechanisms may not be clear, user interfaces should make the security state apparent, similar to how browsers display a lock icon during secure connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Calendars hold private information, so you have to check that the right person is asking for it, make sure the message really came from who it says it did, and watch out for fake invitations and spam.
